title: The month of Phagun
hookLine: in Phagun bliss comes, the Friend revealed (Barah Maha, ang 136)

lines: HALF A LAUGH, HALF A CRY.
cards: There's a particular sound at an airport arrivals gate. Someone has waited a long time, checking the board, rereading the same text. Then the doors slide open, and they see the face.
The sound they make isn't a word. It's half a laugh and half a cry, and everyone nearby turns and smiles. Phagun, roughly mid-February to mid-March, is when Punjab's winter breaks.
Mustard is in flower, the days warm, and in the Barah Maha, after a year of longing, the doors finally open.

teach.b: The stanza opens phalgun anand upaarjanaa, har sajan pragate aa-e. In paraphrase: in Phagun, bliss springs up; the Lord, the Friend, has appeared.
Anand is bliss, deep joy, the same word that names Guru Amar Das's hymn Anand Sahib. Upaarjanaa is to arise, to be produced.
Sajan is a friend, a dear one, someone you love. Pragate aa-e: has come, made visible. After all those months far away, here He is, revealed.

Notice who brings it about: the saints, the Lord's helpers, in their kindness, have brought about the meeting. That's the holy company of Assu and Maghar, still at work. Then the stanza fills with celebration.
The bed is beautiful, every comfort is here, and now there's no room for sorrow. Her wish is fulfilled.
Friends gather and sing songs of joy, the songs of the Lord of the world. And a quiet line: no one else like the Lord can be seen; there's no other to compare with Him.

Phagun is a season of spring festivals. Around Holi, Sikhs gather at Anandpur Sahib for Hola Mohalla, which Sikh tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh: color, music, a crowd. The Barah Maha's bliss isn't private.
It's a party with friends. And there's a lesson in the order. Joy was already there in Chet, the first month, in remembering.
But the meeting itself comes last, after doubt, longing, honesty and humility. The poem doesn't treat those months as wasted. They led here.

how: On the Sangrand of Phagun many gurdwaras read the Phagun stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; around the same season Sikhs gather at Anandpur Sahib for Hola Mohalla, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.

o: a festival of colors held at Anandpur Sahib
the spring month of fasting before Holi
the last month, when the Friend appears

games.q: the month of Phagun — tap the pairs.

s: in the Barah Maha, the Friend is revealed in the first month
the meeting comes in Phagun, the last month of the year, after doubt, longing, honesty and humility.
the stanza says the saints helped bring the meeting about
the Lord's helpers, in kindness, brought the bride and the Friend together.
the stanza's joy is kept private
friends gather and sing songs of joy together.

games.q: after a year of longing, the Friend appears in Phagun. what does the bride do?
o: keep it quiet in case it doesn't last.
gather friends and sing songs of joy.
games.why: the stanza fills with celebration: friends gather and sing songs of the Lord of the world. Phagun's bliss is shared.

practice: Look back over the last few days and find one thing that went right, however small: a warm call, a good meal, a task finished, a moment of laughter.

Let yourself actually enjoy it again, smiling if you like, and think who would be glad to hear it, because Phagun's joy is shared. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between breaths, or hum a line of a shabad you love.

wordCard.voice: Phagun. In the Barah Maha, Phagun is the last month of the year and the month of meeting: bliss springs up, and the Friend is revealed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss. The same word names Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib and the city of Anandpur.

carryVoice: Your line: phagun: bliss. Joy like this is meant for company. Day five hundred seventy-seven, and the doors open.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Phagun stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136)
